Level 1 (Level 2: Intermediate): I-SAPS 'Level 2 Reading List Final.docx' (partner-supplied, 2026-10-26), 13 mandatory readings; the one edit is the first Module 2 author, which the document split into two ('Helen, M., Immordino-Yang, M. H.'). Both are the MANDATORY lists, with the section to read, rationale and outcome. Supplementary readings are shared by I-SAPS as a separate Word document, not listed here. Level 0 replaced the Sept 2026 'Reading Resources Level 1' recommended list (95 items).

1.title: Changing Education Paradigms (TED Talk / RSA Animate, 2010)
1.author: Sir Ken Robinson
1.rationale: Robinson’s talk invites participants to question how standardised schooling shapes assumptions about intelligence, creativity and learner difference. It supports the module’s examination of educational purposes by highlighting divergent thinking and the limitations of uniform approaches to learning.
1.outcome: Differentiate between divergent and convergent thinking; critique factory-model schooling as an outdated and harmful approach that stifles creativity and divergent thinking, marginalizes the arts and treats students as products to be standardized rather than individuals to be nurtured.

1.title: The New Meaning of Educational Change (4th ed.)
1.author: Michael Fullan
1.section: Chapter 2: Shared Meaning and Program Coherence (pp. 37–40); Chapter 3: Capacity Building (pp. 58–61)
1.rationale: Fullan’s work situates educational improvement within the relationships between teacher learning, institutional culture and wider systems. It helps participants understand why capacity building and collective commitment are essential to meaningful change.
1.outcome: Evaluate the importance of teachers’ capacity building.

2.title: Emotional Intelligence (1995)
2.author: Daniel Goleman
2.rationale: A foundational reference on the role of emotional awareness and emotional safety in learning. Goleman’s work introduces emotional awareness and regulation as important dimensions of learning and relationships. It helps participants consider how emotions, including fear and anxiety, influence attention, participation and learners’ readiness to engage.
2.outcome: Explain how fear and anxiety function as "essential guides" in learning contexts.

2.title: Let's Teach for Mastery — Not Test Scores (TED Talk, 2015)
2.author: Sal Khan
2.rationale: This TED Talk challenges assumptions about student ability and argues for mastery-oriented learning. Khan’s talk challenges fixed judgements of ability by showing the importance of time, support and opportunities to master learning. It encourages participants to interpret difficulty as a reason to investigate learning needs and provide further support.
2.outcome: Argue against the assumption that non-participation means lack of ability.

3.title: Discipline and Group Management in Classrooms (1970)
3.author: Jacob Kounin
3.rationale: A foundational text on classroom management, emphasising withitness, momentum and smoothness rather than reactive discipline. Kounin’s work explains how teacher awareness, smooth transitions and sustained lesson momentum support proactive classroom management. It helps participants understand how coordinated classroom activity can maintain engagement and prevent disruptions from escalating.
3.outcome: Explain that Kounin's theory shifts classroom management from reactive discipline to proactive prevention, using research-based techniques like withitness and overlapping that reduce disruptions before they escalate.

3.title: Classroom Management That Works (2003)
3.author: Robert Marzano
3.section: The "Action Steps" sections of Chapter 2 (Rules and Procedures) and Chapter 4 (Teacher-Student Relationships)
3.rationale: A research synthesis examining effective classroom management strategies and their impact. It connects effective classroom management with clear rules and procedures, appropriate responses to behaviour and strong teacher–student relationships, and helps participants understand how predictable expectations and student responsibility contribute to a supportive learning environment.
3.outcome: Implement rules, procedures and disciplinary interventions as part of classroom management, and analyze the importance of student relationships and student responsibility for effective classroom management.

4.title: Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge: A Framework for Teacher Knowledge (2006)
4.author: Punya Mishra and Matthew Koehler
4.rationale: The original paper introducing the TPACK framework. It explains why effective technology integration requires attention to subject content, pedagogy and the relationships between them, and helps participants select digital tools according to their contribution to learning goals and classroom needs.
4.outcome: Move beyond simply using technology to integrating it meaningfully with content and pedagogy, so that digital tools enhance rather than distract from student learning.

5.title: An Introduction to Assessment: The Basics
5.rationale: This resource establishes assessment as a process that guides learning and provides evidence for improving instruction. It helps participants connect learning goals and levels of cognitive demand with appropriate assessment methods.
5.outcome: Align Bloom’s taxonomy with assessment criteria.

5.title: Formative Assessments: Using Feedback to Guide Instruction
5.rationale: This video offers an accessible entry point into the relationship between formative assessment, feedback and responsive teaching. It helps participants understand why feedback should identify learners’ next steps and guide instructional adjustments.

6.title: The Beautiful Risk of Education (2013)
6.author: Gert Biesta
6.rationale: Biesta contrasts learning with subjectification in these pages. His distinction between qualification, socialisation and subjectification broadens learner development beyond acquiring knowledge and meeting prescribed outcomes, and helps participants consider how teaching can support independent judgement and responsible action through relationships that remain open to learners’ responses.
6.outcome: Argue that education is not a risk-free, predictable process of producing outcomes, but a relational encounter that must nurture students' subjectification: their capacity to think and act for themselves.

7.title: Teachers as Cultural Workers: Letters to Those Who Dare Teach (1994)
7.author: Paulo Freire
7.section: The Fourth Letter: "Qualities of the Progressive Teacher Necessary for Better Performance"
7.rationale: Explores qualities and virtues associated with teaching, including humility, tolerance, decisiveness and joy. Freire grounds teaching in ethical commitment and responsive relationships, and helps participants understand how these dispositions support dialogue, learner agency and the responsible exercise of teacher authority.
7.outcome: Explain that education is an act of hope and moral commitment, sustaining belief in the transformative power of teaching even amid systemic challenges and uncertainty.

8.title: The Conditions of Learning (1985)
8.author: Robert Gagné
8.rationale: Introduces the Nine Events of Instruction, a foundational framework for structured lesson sequencing. Gagné’s work provides a framework for organising instruction around the conditions that support learning, and helps participants sequence attention, recall, guidance, practice and feedback to support understanding, retention and transfer.
8.outcome: Use a systematic, research-based framework for sequencing instruction that aligns with how the brain processes and retains new information.

9.title: The Power of Teacher Leadership to Build Collaboration
9.rationale: This resource introduces collaboration as a central expression of teacher leadership through shared expertise, professional dialogue and collective responsibility. It helps participants recognise how everyday contributions to colleagues’ learning can support school improvement.
9.outcome: Build collaboration among team members to strengthen their leadership skills.

1.title: Experience and Education (1938/1997)
1.author: Dewey, J.
1.rationale: Dewey’s Experience and Education provides a philosophical foundation for examining how experience becomes meaningful learning through reflection and inquiry. It helps participants distinguish experiences that support growth and future learning from those that limit them.
1.outcome: Equip themselves with criteria to distinguish genuinely educative experiences from merely activity-filled ones, grounding instruction in inquiry that connects to students' lived experience.

2.title: We Feel, Therefore We Learn: The Relevance of Affective and Social Neuroscience to Education (2007)
2.author: Immordino-Yang, M. H., & Damasio, A.
2.rationale: This article supports the module’s integration of cognitive and affective development by explaining how emotion is intertwined with attention, memory, learning and decision-making. It helps participants understand how learners’ emotional experiences influence their willingness to participate, persist through difficulty and attempt challenging tasks again. It is particularly relevant to discussions of participation and persistence, Sameer’s withdrawal and re-entry, and the relationship between emotional safety and intellectual challenge.
2.outcome: Explain how emotional experiences influence learners’ participation, persistence and engagement with challenging tasks, and identify ways to support both emotional safety and intellectual challenge in the classroom.

2.title: Funds of Knowledge for Teaching: Using a Qualitative Approach to Connect Homes and Classrooms (1992)
2.author: Moll, L. C., Amanti, C., Neff, D., & Gonzalez, N.
2.rationale: Moll et al.’s Funds of Knowledge for Teaching explores how teachers can identify the knowledge and skills accumulated within households and use these resources to develop classroom learning. It provides a foundation for connecting learners’ home and community experiences with disciplinary knowledge. This is particularly relevant to Scene 6, where Sameer’s father contributes his practical knowledge of construction to a Physics lesson. Recognizing this expertise not only enriches learning but can also affirm a learner’s dignity and sense of belonging.
2.outcome: Identify knowledge and skills within learners’ households and communities and use these as resources for meaningful classroom learning.

2.title: The Prosocial Classroom: Teacher Social and Emotional Competence in Relation to Student and Classroom Outcomes (2009)
2.author: Jennings, P. A., & Greenberg, M. T.
2.rationale: This review supports the module’s integration of affective development by examining how teachers’ social and emotional competence and well-being shape supportive teacher–student relationships, classroom management and the implementation of social and emotional learning. It also explores how emotional stress and burnout can undermine classroom relationships and classroom climate. It is particularly relevant to the discussion of teachers’ emotional labour, the effects of workload and leadership on teachers’ well-being, and the challenges of sustaining emotionally responsive teaching.
2.outcome: Explain how teachers’ social and emotional competence and well-being influence classroom relationships and learning, and identify ways school leadership and organisational support can help sustain emotionally responsive teaching.

3.title: Discipline and Group Management in Classrooms (1970)
3.author: Kounin, J. S.
3.rationale: Kounin’s work grounds classroom management in teachers’ awareness, coordination and pacing of classroom activity. It helps participants understand how withitness, overlapping, momentum, smoothness and group focus sustain engagement and prevent disruptions from escalating.
3.outcome: Use Kounin's group management strategies, including withitness, overlapping, and momentum, to create a classroom environment where disruptions are prevented before they escalate.

4.title: The SAMR Model: A Critical Review and Suggestions for Its Use (2016)
4.author: Hamilton, E. R., Rosenberg, J. M., & Akcaoglu, M.
4.rationale: This critical review supports the Digital Literacy module by encouraging thoughtful use of SAMR in relation to learning goals, classroom context and teaching processes. It helps participants evaluate technology’s educational contribution without assuming that movement towards transformation necessarily improves learning.
4.outcome: Analyze a lesson plan using the SAMR model and redesign tasks to move from enhancement to transformation levels.

5.title: The Handbook for Embedded Formative Assessment
5.rationale: The Handbook for Embedded Formative Assessment grounds this module in practical strategies for using evidence of learning to inform teaching and learners’ next steps. It explores how teachers can clarify learning intentions and success criteria, elicit evidence of learning, provide feedback that moves learning forward, activate peer support, and develop learners’ ownership of their learning. Its emphasis on actionable classroom techniques helps teachers translate these strategies into everyday practice.
5.outcome: Select and apply formative assessment techniques to gather evidence of learning, provide useful feedback, and adapt teaching and learning activities to learners’ needs.

5.title: How to Create and Use Rubrics for Formative Assessment and Grading (2013)
5.author: Brookhart, S. M.
5.rationale: Brookhart’s work supports this module by explaining how learning-focused criteria and descriptions of quality make assessment expectations clear and guide improvement. It helps participants select and use analytic or holistic rubrics appropriately for formative assessment and grading.
5.outcome: Design and use effective rubrics that support both formative assessment and fair grading by clearly describing levels of performance and guiding student improvement.

6.title: Mind in Society (1978)
6.author: Vygotsky, L. S.
6.rationale: Vygotsky’s Mind in Society explains how mediation and supported participation within the zone of proximal development enable learners to develop capabilities they cannot yet exercise independently. It helps participants understand how responsive guidance can support increasing independence.
6.outcome: Apply Vygotsky’s concepts of the Zone of Proximal Development and socially mediated learning to design instructional support that helps students progress from assisted to independent performance.

7.title: Project-Based Learning for the 21st Century: Skills for the Future (2010)
7.author: Bell, S.
7.rationale: Bell’s article supports this module by connecting project-based learning with inquiry, collaboration, communication and the creation of authentic products. It helps participants understand how purposeful projects can integrate subject knowledge with critical thinking, problem-solving and learner independence.
7.outcome: Design and implement project-based learning experiences that develop 21st-century skills such as collaboration, critical thinking, communication, and problem-solving through authentic, student-centered inquiry.

8.title: Enhancing Teaching Through Constructive Alignment (1996)
8.author: Biggs, J.
8.rationale: Biggs’s constructive alignment explains why intended outcomes, teaching activities and assessment must support and require the same kind of learning. It helps participants identify mismatches in lesson planning and establish coherence between what learners are expected to learn, practise and demonstrate.
8.outcome: Apply the principle of constructive alignment by designing teaching activities and assessment tasks that are coherently linked to the intended learning outcomes.

8.title: Principles of Instruction (2012)
8.author: Rosenshine, B.
8.rationale: Rosenshine’s principles provide a research-informed basis for sequencing instruction through review, small steps, modelling, questioning and practice. They help participants plan appropriate support and checks for understanding as learners move from guided to independent practice.
8.outcome: Apply Rosenshine’s principles of instruction, such as daily review, scaffolding, guided practice, and checking for understanding, to design clear, effective, and research-based classroom teaching.

9.title: Gestalt psychology: An introduction to new concepts in modern psychology (1947)
9.author: Köhler, W.
9.rationale: Köhler’s Gestalt psychology offers a lens for understanding how parts acquire meaning through their relationships within a whole. Applied to leadership, it encourages participants to examine how individual actions, relationships and institutional conditions interact to shape school life.
9.outcome: Explain how the human mind naturally organizes complex information into unified, meaningful structures rather than a collection of isolated parts.
